segments.text: Here is an odd fact about air defense.
A battery can pick up an aircraft 400 km away,
track it, identify it and know exactly where it is
and still be unable to do anything about it.
The radar that sees and the missile that kills
are different machines with different ranges
and neither can do the other's job.
A modern air defense system is not one weapon.
It is a conversation between a dozen of them
and if one stops talking, the aircraft keeps coming.
So here is the question.
How does an army stop things that fly fast, low
and from any direction when no single weapon
can cover all of that?
The answer starts with a refusal.
No missile is good at everything.
So air defense is built in layers and each layer is there
because the one beyond it cannot be trusted
to catch everything.
Start with the long layer, large missile systems
of the type that sit around a capital or a major base
can reach out 100 km or more
with the biggest advertised well beyond that.
They are the only layer that can engage a bomber before it releases its weapons
or a ballistic missile on the way down.
They are also big, costly and slow to move
and there are never enough of them.
A battery carries a limited number of missiles ready to fire
and each costs more than a house.
So the long layer is a precious thing that nobody wants to waste on a cheap target.
That sets up the next layer.
If the big missile is too good to spend on small things, something cheaper has to take the middle ground.
Medium range systems reach 30 or 50 commoters, use smaller missiles and move on trucks.
They cover an army in the field or a city and they are where most of the shooting happens.
They have a flaw of their own which is that they depend on a radar and a radar does not work against what it cannot see.
A low flying aircraft or a missile skimming the ground can sit below the radar's view because the curve of the earth hides it until it is close.
This is the real reason low flying works.
Radar travels in a straight line and the earth is round, so a target at 50 meters altitude can be invisible to a radar until it is a few dozen kimoners away.
The aircraft is not hiding in a clever way, it is hiding behind the planet, so the layers are completed from the ground up.
At the short end, there are guns and small missiles on armored vehicles that move with the troops and at the shortest are shoulder-fired missiles that one soldier carries and aims by eye.
One answer to the round earth is to lift the radar.
A large aircraft with a rotating dish above its fuselage flies at high altitude and sees low flying targets from far beyond the horizon that blinds a ground radar.
It is expensive and there are few of them, but it explains why air campaigns begin by going after the sensors because a defense that cannot see low has to guess.
Shoulder missiles are worth a closer look because they invert the logic.
They cost a fraction of a jet, need no radar, and are carried by a person who can stand in a ditch.
They reach only a few commoders, and the missile finds its target by the heat of the engine.
Low flying aircraft and helicopters avoid the places where they might be, and so a soldier with a tube changes where a whole air force dares to fly.
The value of such a weapon is less in what it shoots than in what the enemy decides not to do.
How a missile finds its target decides how a layer can be used.
Some are steered from the ground by the same radar that tracks the target, which means the radar has to keep looking until the very end.
Others carry their own small radar in the nose and finish the chase alone, which frees the ground radar to turn to the next target.
Heat-seeking ones need nothing but the engine's glow.
The more the missile does for itself, the more targets a battery can handle at once, and the more it costs.
Speed is the next constraint.
A jet at 500 meters a second crosses 30 commoters in a minute, so a crew that sees it at the edge of its range has a window that is not long.
In that minute, someone has to decide that the contact is hostile, choose a missile and fire.
Automation does most of it, and a human often only has a veto.
The faster the threats, the less a person is the one deciding, and the more the real choices happen in the weeks before, when the rules are written.
Now something has to hold these layers together, because a ship's captain, a battery commander and an infantry platoon cannot shout at one another.
This is the command network, and it is the least visible part and the most important.
Sensors across a region feed one picture, and the network decides which battery takes which target,
so that two batteries do not fire at one aircraft while another one slips through.
Without it, the layers are just separate pieces.
With it, each layer covers the gaps in the others.
The network is what turns a collection of weapons into a system.
Deciding who is hostile is its own danger.
Radar sees a shape, and a shape does not wear a flag.
Aircraft carry a transponder that answers a coded challenge, but codes fail and radios break.
In 2003, during the invasion of Iraq, American patriot batteries shot down a British tornado and a US Navy fighter,
both friendly, because the system took them for missiles.
The same networks that make a layered defense strong also make a mistake travel quickly.
And every part of this system has one thing in common, which is that it gives itself away.
A radar that sends out a signal can be heard and found, and there are missiles that fly down the beam to destroy it.
So radars switch on for short periods and then move, a practice called shoot and scoot,
and some are decoyed by cheap transmitters that make the enemy think a battery is somewhere it is not.
An air defense unit that stays on all day is a unit that is about to be hit.
The system survives by being intermittent.
There is a famous example from 1960.
An American high-altitude spy plane, the U-2, flew over the Soviet Union for years because nothing could reach it.
Then a Soviet missile battery, using radar-guided missiles that explode when they pass close to the target, shot one down.
The pilot survived and was put on trial.
That event also shows the scale of the contest.
For years, the defense was a step behind the aircraft, and then, within the space of one afternoon, it wasn't.
The deepest problem is arithmetic, though.
A missile is a precision weapon that costs a lot, and what it shoots at may be a cheap drone or a decoy.
If the attacker spends a little and the defender spends a lot, the defender loses even when every shot hits.
This is why more and more air defense is pushed to cheaper kinds, guns that throw out thousands of small, cheap shells,
jammers that cost almost nothing per use, and in some places, lasers that cost little more than electricity.
Each is limited in range or in weather, but they change the cost of the exchange.
Even a perfect battery has a limit, which is how many missiles it holds.
Launchers carry a few ready rounds, and a reload takes a vehicle, a crane, and a crew.
An attacker who sends a large raid at once is not trying to get every missile through.
They are trying to make the battery empty, so the next wave meets nothing.
The defender's real number is not the range of the missile.
It is the number of rounds left at the moment the second wave arrives.
Numbers matter here, too.
The attacker chooses the time, the place, and the number, and can send a hundred things at one point,
where the defender has to cover a whole country. A defense that is excellent everywhere is impossible.
What the defender can do is protect a few things very well, and accept that the rest will be hit.
That is not defeatism, but an honest accounting.
The choices about what to protect are made long before the first alarm,
and they say a great deal about what a state thinks matters.
Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong.
People measure air defense by how many aircraft it shoots down.
A better measure might be how many it prevents from coming.
A pilot who has to fly low, take a long way round, or turn back,
is a pilot who has been beaten without a missile being fired.
That is my own reading.
But it suggests that the real product of an air defense system is not a kill.
It is a route the enemy does not take.
So return to the radar that sees 400 commodores and the missile that cannot reach that far.
Every layer, the long missile, the medium one, the gun, the shoulder tube,
and the network that links them, exists because no single weapon is enough.
The air defense does not stop the sky from being dangerous.
It makes certain parts of the sky too expensive to enter.
